summary:
A sidebar, **"The validation_split argument"**, offers a shortcut: instead of slicing validation data by hand and passing `validation_data`, you can pass `validation_split` to `fit()`, a fraction of the training data to hold out. With `model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=512, validation_split=0.2)`, 20% of `x_train`/`y_train` is held out from training and used for validation.

Back in the main text: on CPU, training with listing 4.7 takes less than 2 seconds per epoch, so it is done in about 20 seconds; each epoch ends with a short pause while loss and accuracy are computed on the 10,000 validation samples.

`model.fit()` returns a **`History`** object (seen in chapter 3) whose member `history` is a dictionary of everything that happened during training. Its keys are `"accuracy"`, `"loss"`, `"val_accuracy"` and `"val_loss"`: one entry per metric monitored during training and during validation (loss and accuracy, each for both sets).

The next two listings plot these with Matplotlib: training vs validation loss (figure 4.4) and training vs validation accuracy (figure 4.5). The authors warn your own numbers may differ slightly because of random weight initialization. **Listing 4.8** starts on this page: it extracts `loss_values` and `val_loss_values`, builds `epochs = range(1, len(loss_values) + 1)`, plots training loss as `"r--"` (dashed red line) and validation loss as `"b"` (solid blue line), sets the title `"[IMDB] Training and validation loss"` and the x-label `"Epochs"`. The listing continues on p.137, where figure 4.4 is shown.

concepts.name: validation_split vs validation_data
concepts.definition: Two ways to provide held-out data to fit(): an explicit (x, y) tuple, or a fraction of the training arrays.
concepts.intuition: Either hand Keras the practice exam, or let it tear off the last 20% of the textbook for one.
concepts.significance: Both feed val_ metrics into History.
concepts.misconception: validation_split does not shuffle before splitting.

concepts.name: History object
concepts.definition: The return value of fit(); history.history is a dict of per-epoch metric values.
concepts.technical: Keys here: accuracy, loss, val_accuracy, val_loss; each a list of length 20.
concepts.misconception: It does not store the model weights per epoch.

concepts.name: Training and validation curves
concepts.definition: Plots of loss/metrics per epoch for training and validation data.
concepts.significance: Primary diagnostic for choosing the number of epochs.
concepts.misconception: Small differences between runs are normal due to random init.

code.title: Plotting the training and validation loss (first part; continues on p.137)
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

history_dict = history.history
loss_values = history_dict["loss"]
val_loss_values = history_dict["val_loss"]
epochs = range(1, len(loss_values) + 1)
plt.plot(epochs, loss_values, "r--", label="Training loss")
plt.plot(epochs, val_loss_values, "b", label="Validation loss")
plt.title("[IMDB] Training and validation loss")
plt.xlabel("Epochs")
code.what_it_does: Extracts per-epoch losses and plots training loss (dashed red) and validation loss (solid blue) against epoch number. The remaining lines of the listing are on p.137.

line_explanations.explanation: Gets the training and validation loss lists.
"r--" is for "dashed red line" (book callout): training loss.
"b" is for "solid blue line" (book callout): validation loss.

deeper.title: Why training and validation metrics are not perfectly comparable
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the training loss recorded for an epoch is the average over its batches, computed while the weights were still changing; early batches used worse weights. The validation loss is computed once with the final weights of the epoch. So in early epochs validation loss can even be lower than training loss without anything being wrong.

deeper.title: What history_dict looks like
deeper.body: Illustration (not from the book): `history_dict["loss"]` is a list such as `[0.52, 0.31, 0.23, ...]` of length 20, and `history_dict["val_accuracy"]` a list of 20 accuracies. The actual numbers on your machine will vary with random initialization, as the authors note.

visualizations.title: What the four History curves typically look like
visualizations.why: Listing 4.8 is about to plot training vs validation loss for 20 epochs; this generic simulation (not the book's data) shows the shape to watch for.

misconceptions.claim: validation_split=0.2 here yields the same 10,000-sample validation set as listing 4.6.
misconceptions.correction: 20% of 25,000 is 5,000 samples, taken from the end of the arrays.

misconceptions.claim: History contains only the training loss.
misconceptions.correction: It has one entry per monitored metric for both training and validation: four here.

misconceptions.claim: Your curves should exactly match the book's.
misconceptions.correction: The authors note results vary slightly due to random initialization.

questions.question: Which keys does history.history contain for the IMDb model?
questions.explanation: One entry per metric for training and validation. Only loss would omit accuracy; there are no test_ keys; optimizer names are not metrics.

questions.question: Why does the book warn your results may vary slightly?
questions.answer: Because the model's weights are randomly initialized, so each run follows a slightly different training trajectory.
